intro.html: Big and small are the first describing words children learn; these ten are their grown-up cousins. Five are for the enormous (immense, colossal, monumental, prodigious, gargantuan) and five for the tiny (minute, minuscule, diminutive, infinitesimal, negligible).
Each has a flavor. Monumental and prodigious often mean great in importance or skill, not just size. Diminutive usually describes a person. Negligible means so small it doesn’t matter.
Two traps: minuscule is spelled with a u (from minus), and minute the adjective is pronounced my-NOOT, not like the minute on a clock.

words.ex: The blue whale is an {immense} animal, longer than two school buses.
words.ctx: Looking out from the plane, she was struck by how {immense} the desert was: hour after hour, nothing but sand in every direction.

mn.text: Kai tries to measure the whale with his little ruler and gives up after the tail. It is {immense}: too big to measure.

scene.alt: A boy in a rowboat holds up a tiny ruler beside an enormous whale.

words.def: enormous; huge enough to fill you with awe
words.ex: A {colossal} statue towered over the harbor, dwarfing the ships below.
words.ctx: The project was a {colossal} undertaking: three thousand workers, ten years and enough steel to build a small city.
words.etym: From colossus, a gigantic statue, from Greek kolossos; the most famous was the huge bronze Colossus that stood at the harbor of Rhodes.

mn.cue: COLOSSUS: a statue so big it awes
mn.text: The giant statue at the harbor is so tall that the sailing ships look like toys at its feet. It is {colossal}.

scene.alt: A gigantic statue towers over a tiny girl and a small sailboat in the harbor.

words.def: very great in size or importance
words.ex: Finishing the five-thousand-piece puzzle was a {monumental} task.
words.ctx: The discovery of the cure was a {monumental} achievement, one that historians still rank among the most important of the century.

roots.means: a means or result (a noun ending)

words.etym: From monument, from Latin monumentum, “a reminder, a memorial,” from monere (to remind).

mn.cue: MONUMENT-al: as big as a MONUMENT
mn.text: After a whole summer, Lila fits the last of five thousand puzzle pieces into place. Finishing it was a {monumental} task.

scene.alt: A girl cheers as she finishes a giant five-thousand-piece puzzle.

words.ex: Professor Edwin owns a {prodigious} library, with books stacked to the ceiling.
words.ctx: The young violinist had a {prodigious} memory: she could hear a long piece once and play it back the next day without a single wrong note.
words.etym: From Latin prodigiosus, “wondrous,” from prodigium, “a wonder, an omen,” the source of prodigy.

mn.cue: PRODIGY-ous: a wonder of a size
mn.text: Professor Edwin’s books are stacked from the floor to the ceiling, so he needs a ladder to reach the top. His library is {prodigious}.

labels.text: PRODIGY-ous: a WONDER of a size

scene.alt: A professor on a ladder reaches for the top of towering stacks of books.

words.def: enormous, especially in bulk or appetite
words.ex: Omar grew a {gargantuan} watermelon that took four people to lift.
words.ctx: The puppy’s appetite was {gargantuan}: it finished its own bowl, the cat’s bowl and half a loaf of bread before anyone noticed.
words.etym: From Gargantua, a jolly giant with an enormous appetite in a French comic tale of the 1500s.

mn.text: Omar grows a watermelon so big that the whole family has to push to roll it out of the garden. It is {gargantuan}.

scene.alt: A man and a boy push an enormous watermelon across the garden.

words.ex: A {minute} speck of dust jammed the old watch.
words.ctx: The scientist examined the leaf in {minute} detail, recording every tiny vein, spot and hair that most people would never notice.
words.etym: From Latin minutus, “made small,” from minuere (to lessen).
words.note: The adjective is pronounced my-NOOT. The noun minute (MIN-it), a sixtieth of an hour, comes from the same Latin word: a “small part.”

mn.text: Zoe’s pet newt is so tiny it fits on a fingertip; she needs a magnifying glass to see its toes. Her newt is {minute}.

scene.alt: A girl kneels with a magnifying glass to see a tiny newt on a leaf.

words.ex: Split among ten friends, the last cookie became ten {minuscule} crumbs.
words.ctx: The difference in price was {minuscule}, just two cents, so Grandma bought the pears from the farmer she liked best.
words.etym: From Latin minuscula (littera), “rather small (letter),” from minus (less).
words.note: Spelled with a u, from minus. “Miniscule” is a common misspelling.

mn.cue: MINUS-cule: so small it’s almost a MINUS
mn.text: The last cookie is shared with eight friends, and Ivy squints at her share: one crumb. It is {minuscule}.

scene.alt: A girl squints at the tiny crumb of cookie that is her share.

words.ex: The {diminutive} coach barely reached her players’ shoulders, but they hung on her every word.
words.ctx: Though {diminutive} in size, the old pony was the boss of the barn; even the giant draft horses stepped aside for him.
words.etym: From Latin diminutus, “made smaller,” from deminuere (to lessen), the same source as diminish.
words.note: In grammar, a diminutive is a form that means “little”: duckling, booklet.

mn.text: Nana Lou, barely five feet tall, coaches a team of giants, and they all listen when she blows her whistle. She is {diminutive} but mighty.

scene.alt: A tiny grandmother coach with a whistle stands between two very tall players.

words.ex: Under the microscope, Sami found {infinitesimal} creatures swimming in a drop of pond water.
words.ctx: The difference between the two scales was {infinitesimal}, less than the weight of a grain of sand, so the baker trusted either one.
words.etym: From Modern Latin infinitesimus, “the infinitieth (part),” from infinitus (endless).

mn.text: Sami peers into the microscope at creatures so small that no ruler could ever measure them. They are {infinitesimal}.

scene.alt: A boy in a lab coat looks through a microscope at creatures too small to measure.

words.def: so small or unimportant it can be ignored
words.ex: Pouring one cup of water into the ocean has a {negligible} effect on its level.
words.ctx: The repair added a {negligible} amount to the bill, only a dollar, so the shop owner simply didn’t charge for it.

mn.text: Pip pours one bucket of water into the ocean and checks whether the sea has risen. The difference is {negligible}: small enough to ignore.

scene.alt: A boy on the dock pours a bucket of water into the sea and wonders if it rose.

after.html: Minute has two pronunciations and two meanings. MIN-it is the sixty-second minute; my-NOOT means tiny, or carefully detailed (a minute examination). Both come from Latin minutus, “made small.”

items.why: Minuscule comes from Latin minus, “less,” so it is spelled with a u.

items.q: In “The detective made a minute search of the room,” minute means…
items.why: Minute (my-NOOT) can mean very detailed; a minute search looks at the tiniest things.

choices: cannot be measured because it is so large
items.why: Negligible means so small it can be neglected, or ignored.

items.q: True or false: a colossal statue would fit in your pocket.
items.why: False. Colossal means enormous, like the giant statue called a colossus.
